name: Piano & Guitar Fundamentals Reboot

tempo.note: Hanon target: 60 bpm in week 1, +5 each week

phases.name: Technical rebuild
phases.piano: Hanon, all 12 major scales, triads and inversions, 10 minutes of sight-reading every session. Maple Leaf Rag stays closed.
phases.guitar: CAGED as five moveable shapes, the major scale laid over each one, triads built from root–3rd–5th, and rhythm work.

phases.name: Applied theory
phases.piano: Left-hand patterns (block, Alberti, stride), cadences in every key you have covered, and Maple Leaf Rag rebuilt strain by strain.
phases.guitar: Minor pentatonic across five boxes, chord-tone targeting, and two modes that actually earn their keep: Mixolydian and Dorian.

phases.name: Improvisation
phases.piano: Left-hand vamp, right hand improvising — pentatonic, then the blues scale, then ii–V–I with chord tones as targets.
phases.guitar: 12-bar blues in A, then the major/minor pentatonic hybrid and call-and-response, then the blues in E and G.

keysNote: The plan says two new keys a week and all 12 by week 4; three a week is what gets there. Order follows the fingering groups: C G D A E, then F B♭ E♭, then B F♯ D♭ A♭.

1.detail: Map out every F major using each shape — same chord, five places on the neck.

2.detail: Same drill: find the root, then the shape, then the chord.

3.detail: Then lay all five shapes for G major end to end up the neck and see how they overlap.

4.detail: Play a I–IV–V progression in one key using a different CAGED shape for each chord, so you are forced to move instead of staying in one spot.

theory.d: Name and hear every interval inside the octave. From any given note, play the note a major 3rd above, a perfect 5th above, and so on, until it is instant. Then start building major scales from W–W–H–W–W–W–H.
Keep deriving the 12 major scales from the formula rather than recalling key signatures. For each one, immediately build its relative natural minor. Start memorising C–G–D–A–E–B–F♯–D♭–A♭–E♭–B♭–F.

theory.t: Circle of fifths into diatonic harmony
theory.d: Circle to instant recall, then stack thirds on each degree: I ii iii IV V vi vii°. Every progression you know is a path through tonic → subdominant → dominant → tonic.
Add a third on top of each triad: maj7, dom7, min7, m7♭5, dim7. The first three are the ones you will use constantly in stride voicings and blues comping.

Applied now, not studied. Major → major scale, major pentatonic, Lydian or Mixolydian. Dominant 7th → Mixolydian or the blues scale. Minor → Dorian, natural minor, minor pentatonic. Hear and play ii–V–I in C, G and F.

5.d: Hands separately, then together at half tempo. Four-bar chunks with the metronome; only move the tempo up once a chunk is clean.

6.t: Maple Leaf Rag — Strain A up to tempo, Strain B hands separate
6.d: The form is AABBACCD, so A has to be reliable before B goes anywhere.

7.t: Maple Leaf Rag — Strain B up to tempo, add Strain C
7.d: Same four-bar chunking. The stride left hand is the engine here.

8.t: Maple Leaf Rag — full run-through, add Strain D
8.d: Whole piece plus tempo work. You already have much of this in muscle memory.

9.t: Pentatonic improv over a left-hand vamp
9.d: Left hand: root–5th, or a two-chord I–V loop in C. Right hand improvises on C major pentatonic (C–D–E–G–A) only — no wrong notes available.

10.d: Same vamp in C. Leave space, repeat a motif, answer it. The restriction is still C major pentatonic.

11.t: Blues scale over a 12-bar left hand
11.d: C blues scale (C–E♭–F–F♯–G–B♭) over a 12-bar blues pattern in C.

12.t: ii–V–I with chord tones as targets
12.d: Dm7–G7–Cmaj7 vamp in the left hand. Right hand targets the 3rd and 7th of each chord instead of running the scale — this is what separates playing changes from noodling.

9.d: A7–D7–E7. A minor pentatonic only. Phrasing is the point: leave space, repeat motifs, do not run the scale up and down. Record yourself.

10.t: 12-bar blues in A — phrasing and recording
10.d: Same progression. Listen back to last session's recording first, then play against it.

11.d: Mix major and minor pentatonic over the I chord. Play a 2-bar lick, leave a 2-bar gap, answer it with a variation.

12.t: Blues in E and G, connecting boxes
12.d: Two new keys, and connect two adjacent pentatonic positions instead of staying in one box — this is what stops a solo sounding stuck.

1.title: Hanon 1–5
1.detail: Hands separate first, then together, with the metronome.

1.title: Major scales, 2 octaves, hands together
1.detail: New this week: {keys}. Keep the earlier keys in rotation.

1.title: Triads and inversions — {keys}
1.detail: Root position, 1st inversion, 2nd inversion. Hands separate, then together.

1.title: Sight-reading — something you have never seen
1.detail: A hymnal, a graded method book around RCM/ABRSM grade 3–5, or public-domain sheet music. This is the slow-reading gap.

2.title: Hanon 1–5 — maintenance
2.detail: Keep the hands warm and the tempo climbing.

2.title: Left-hand accompaniment patterns
2.detail: Block chords, then Alberti bass (root–5th–3rd–5th), then stride (bass note on 1 and 3, chord on 2 and 4). Stride is literally the Maple Leaf Rag left hand.

2.title: Cadences — I–IV–V–I, hands together
2.detail: In every key you have covered. This is where Part 1 harmony gets into your fingers.

3.title: Maintenance — Maple Leaf Rag and one or two pieces you love
3.detail: Ten minutes, so nothing you have already built goes rusty.

1.title: Major scale in position
1.detail: For each CAGED shape you know, learn the major scale pattern that overlays it. Box-based fingering first — it is the standard for rock, blues and improv.

1.title: Build the chord, don't recall the shape
1.detail: For each triad, physically find the root, the 3rd and the 5th on the fretboard. This is what lets you play chord-tone-aware lines later.

1.title: Rhythm — 8ths, 16ths, syncopation
1.detail: Strong rhythm is what makes basic improv sound intentional rather than random.

2.title: Minor pentatonic in the five boxes
2.detail: Start in A minor pentatonic — no sharps or flats, so it is the clean reference point. The minor pentatonic is 1–♭3–4–5–♭7 of the natural minor.

2.title: Chord-tone targeting
2.detail: Over a static Cmaj7, run the scale but land deliberately on a chord tone (C, E, G or B) on beat 1 of each bar. This single drill will do the most for how your improv sounds.

2.title: Mixolydian and Dorian
2.detail: Mixolydian = major scale with a ♭7, the sound of dominant-7 rhythm changes. Dorian = natural minor with a raised 6th, the sound of minor-key rock and funk vamps. Learn both against shapes you already know.

3.title: Maintenance — your strongest songs
3.detail: Ten minutes, so the pieces you already own stay owned.

repertoire.picked: The theory you are drilling this week is the theory this song uses.

suggest.1-piano: Something well below your ceiling — River Flows in You, a Clair de Lune excerpt, or a pop ballad.
suggest.2-piano: Autumn Leaves (almost entirely ii–V–I), or any I–V–vi–IV song: Let It Be, Someone Like You.
suggest.3-piano: A lead sheet — melody and chord symbols only — with your own left-hand voicing.
suggest.1-guitar: A song you already half-know, played with barre/CAGED shapes up the neck instead of in open position.
suggest.2-guitar: A blues in A with a known solo — Sweet Home Chicago, or Hendrix/SRV-style. Rhythm part first, then lift bars of the solo by ear.
suggest.3-guitar: A fingerstyle arrangement you love, as the non-improv payoff for the phase.

mon.d: Time one scale run, clean, at this week's tempo — then try to beat it. Accuracy first, speed second.

tue.t: Ten minutes on the repertoire pick
tue.d: No grading, no metronome demands. Just play the song.

thu.t: Ten minutes on the just-for-fun song
thu.d: No metronome. Badly is fine. This is the reset valve, not an exercise.

sat.d: A riff or a hook from a song you love. Figure it out before you look it up.

notes.title: Maple Leaf Rag stays closed until week 5.
notes.detail: Let the technical base rebuild first — you come back to it faster this way.

checkpoint.title: Phase {phase} checkpoint — record yourself
checkpoint.detail: Same simple exercise every time (a scale at target tempo, or a short improvised phrase) so you have a direct before/after. Log it in Progress.

piano: I Guess That's Why They Call It the Blues

reference.title: 1.1 Intervals
reference.html:
Minor 2nd, major 2nd, minor 3rd, major 3rd, perfect 4th, tritone, perfect 5th, minor 6th, major 6th, minor 7th, major 7th, octave.

Drill — from any given note, play the note a major 3rd above it, a perfect 5th above it, and so on. Daily for a week until it is instant. This one skill underlies scale construction, chord construction and improv targeting.

reference.title: 1.2 Major scale construction
reference.html: W–W–H–W–W–W–H. Build all 12 major scales by applying the formula from each of the 12 notes. Derive each one — do not recall the key signature. This is the highest-leverage theory exercise available to you.

reference.title: 1.3 Minor scales
reference.html:
• Natural minor — W–H–W–W–H–W–W, or the 6th degree of the relative major.
  • Harmonic minor — natural minor with a raised 7th; the augmented 2nd gives it that exotic sound.
  • Melodic minor — raised 6th and 7th ascending, natural minor descending. Jazz players often use the ascending form both ways.
Drill — for every major key you build, immediately build its relative natural minor.

reference.title: 1.4 Key signatures and the circle
reference.html: C–G–D–A–E–B–F♯–D♭–A♭–E♭–B♭–F–C. Each step clockwise adds a sharp or removes a flat. This gives you key signatures instantly and is the map for progressions and modulation later.

reference.title: 1.5 Diatonic harmony
reference.html:
Stack thirds on each degree of the major scale.

Every progression you have ever played is some path through tonic → subdominant → dominant → tonic. Once this clicks you can predict progressions by ear and improvise over them with intention instead of guessing.

reference.title: 1.6 Seventh chords
reference.html: Add a third on top of each triad: maj7, dom7, min7, m7♭5 (half-diminished), dim7. You will use maj7, dom7 and min7 constantly — in ragtime voicings and in blues and jazz comping.

reference.title: 1.7 Chord–scale relationships
reference.html:
The theory that directly powers improv.
  • Major chord → major scale, major pentatonic, or Lydian / Mixolydian depending on context
  • Dominant 7th → Mixolydian, or the blues scale
  • Minor chord → Dorian, natural minor, or minor pentatonic
  • ii–V–I → the most common progression in jazz and pop. Learn to hear and play it in every key eventually; start with C, G and F.

principles: Every concept gets attached to a song in the same week.
Learning the I–IV–V cadence is boring in isolation. Learning it because it is the backbone of the blues song you are about to play is not.
One just-for-fun song per phase. No pressure, no metronome.
Separate from the graded repertoire. Pick it because you love it, regardless of whether it fits the curriculum. It is an emotional reset valve, not a skill-building exercise.

Time a scale run and beat it. Work out a song's opening interval by ear before checking. Transcribe one short phrase instead of only reading notation. Leave the pure repetitive grind — intervals, sight-reading reps — to an app with streaks and scores.

If a song excites you more than the correct next technical step, learn the song and reverse-engineer the theory from it. The order here is a default, not a rule. Motivation compounds — chase it when it shows up.
student: Adult rebuilding technique after time away. Piano: reads around RCM/ABRSM grade 3–5 but sight-reads slowly; has played Maple Leaf Rag before. Guitar: knows most open chords and is now learning CAGED shapes, the major scale in position and the pentatonic boxes.
